new_statements.quote: [p.69] Having lost tone in monosyllabic words, Hui people use the accent opposition of high (H) and low (L) in dissyllabic words. ... In Standard Mandarin, this suffix is atonal; in other words, the accent is on the first tonal syllable. However in Tangwang, the situation is reversed, and the suffix must be phonetically put in focus. Among Han people however, the pronunciation is more similar to Standard Mandarin: the suffix ts is not necessarily stressed. [p.70] ...dissyllabic words, the general tendency is LH and not the reverse. [p.76] It is clear that their stress pattern in Dongxiang is the same as in Tangwang (see Table 3.13). The Dongxiang language must have influenced the Tangwang language, a Chinese variety, since the former is a stress-final language while Standard Mandarin...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Among Hui (Muslim) speakers, lexical tone is lost on monosyllables and disyllabic words carry a Low-High accent pattern, i.e. prominence (H accent/stress) on the final syllable, even on the nominal suffix -tsɿ that is toneless/unstressed in Standard Mandarin; the pattern matches stress-final Dongxiang. Han speakers in Tangwang keep a reduced (2-3) tone system and do not necessarily stress the suffix.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: 'general tendency is LH and not the reverse' (so not exceptionless); Han speakers pattern more like Standard Mandarin (suffix -tsɿ not necessarily stressed); speakers told the author context, not stress, disambiguates disyllabic homophones (p.74); one Han informant uses three tones (fn.31).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern disyllabic words in citation/reading forms and a perception test of disyllabic homophones (Tables 3.11-3.13); described as an H/L 'accent' opposition replacing tone rather than classic dynamic stress. Access was via page-numbered Google Books snippets; one snippet sentence reads 'generally the H accent is on the syllable' with a word apparently missing in the printed text, so the LH/final reading rests on pp. 70 and 76.
new_statements.identity_note: Xu 2017 describes the speech of Tangwang town (唐汪川), Dongxiang Autonomous County, Linxia Hui Prefecture, Gansu = Glottolog tang1373. The stress-final/LH statement applies specifically to Hui (Muslim, incl. converted Tang/Wang clans) speakers; Han speakers in the same villages are described as retaining a reduced 2-3-tone system closer to Hezhou/Linxia Mandarin. Djamouri (2022, 2025) treats the same variety as having three low-amplitude contrastive tones and regards the tone-vs-accent question as unresolved.

sources.citation: Djamouri, R., C. Lamarre & J. Lefort. 2025. Introductory perspectives on language contact: Northern Sinitic varieties and neighbouring languages. (HAL hal-05418976)
sources.note: General remark on the role of stress in Northern Chinese contact varieties; nothing specific to Tangwang stress position.

sources.citation: Djamouri, Redouane. 2025/2026. Causative and Applicative in Tangwang: Morphological distinctions and contact-induced restructuration. In Djamouri, Lamarre & Lefort (eds), Language Contact in Northern China. (HAL hal-04874466 preprint; hal-05546801 chapter)
sources.note: States 'there are to date no decisive studies on the number or even the existence of contrastive tones in Tangwang', criticising analyses that disregard 'the accentuation phenomena' words exhibit; cites Ran, Yu & Shi 2022 and Li Lan 2022 for competing tone analyses. No stress-position rule.

sources.citation: Djamouri, Redouane. 2022. Récit en tangwang glosé et annoté. CRLAO ms. (HAL hal-03514315)
sources.note: Explicitly gives no prosodic marking 'qu'elles soient tonales ou accentuelles', pending analysis of sandhi inside 'groupes accentuels' whose limits do not coincide with phrases.
